This page teaches the one pattern that every extraction in the guide follows:
open a register as a lazy connection, filter the rows, select the columns, and
only then fetch the result into R with `collect()`. Read it after [Phase 4 -
File types and loading](file-formats.qmd), where you saw that parquet registers
are opened lazily, and before you try the pattern yourself in [Phase
6](first-extraction.qmd). When you are done you can read any extraction in the
guide, and you can tell whether an object is data in R or still an unsent query.

The reason for the pattern is size. `read_csv()` or `readRDS()` reads the entire
file into memory at once, which works for your own small datasets, but BEF and
LMDB have many millions of rows and would crash your session. A lazy connection
lets you filter before you fetch, so only the rows you need reach memory.

## The pattern: open connection → filter → select → fetch

Think of a supermarket. You can either buy the whole shop and sort at home - or
send a shopping list and only have what is on the list delivered. Lazy loading
is the latter: you describe what you want, and only fetch the items at the end
with `collect()`.

**Step 1 - open the register** as a lazy connection. Pick the way that matches
your project (the rest of the pattern is identical whichever you choose):

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### fastreg (recommended)

```r
library(fastreg)

bef <- read_register("bef") %>% rename_with(tolower)
```

This assumes you have pointed fastreg at your registers with one `options()`
call at the top of the script - see [Point fastreg at your
registers](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#fastreg-paths). That call is not repeated in
the guide's examples: it belongs at the top of the script, once, not before each
read.

#### arrow (any parquet)

```r
library(arrow)
bef <- open_dataset(
  "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/[your-parquet-folder]/bef/"
) %>%
  rename_with(tolower)
```
:::

**Steps 2-3 - filter, select, then fetch.** `bef` is now a lazy connection (no
data has moved). The rest is the same regardless of how you opened it:

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, select, collect

# 2. Filter rows and select columns - still no data in R
bef_filtered <- bef %>%
  filter(year == 2020) %>%
  select(pnr, koen, foed_dag, familie_id)

# 3. collect() - HERE the selected data is moved into R's memory
bef_data <- bef_filtered %>% collect()
```

Steps 1 and 2 are instructions only and cost almost no memory. `collect()` in
step 3 is the only line that moves data.

::: {.callout-note}
**Why `rename_with(tolower)` as the first step?** Column names in DST registers
are not capitalised consistently (`PNR`, `pnr`, `Pnr`). With everything in lower
case from the start, the rest of your code can use `pnr` everywhere. Add it
right after `read_register()` or `open_dataset()`, before you filter or select.
:::

## Filter rows and select columns before `collect()` {#filter-before-collect}

```r
# CORRECT - filter rows and select columns BEFORE collect
result <- large_register %>%
  filter(year == 2020) %>% # keep only the rows you need
  select(pnr, koen, foed_dag) %>% # keep only the columns you use
  collect() # only now is data moved into R

# WRONG - fetches all rows and all columns into RAM first, then filters
result <- large_register %>%
  collect() %>% # everything into RAM - can crash the session
  filter(year == 2020)
```

Calling `collect()` before you have narrowed the rows can crash your session,
and because everyone shares the server's RAM, it slows the server for everyone
else at the same time. The more you filter and select in advance, the faster
and more stably it runs.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Rule of thumb:** `filter()` limits rows. `select()` limits columns. Use both
*before* `collect()`, never after.
:::

### Very large registers: `compute()` instead of `collect()` {#compute-vs-collect}

On the very largest registers (LMDB, laboratory results), even a filtered result
can be too big to pull into R comfortably, or you may need it as the input to
several later queries. Then end the pipe with `compute()` instead of
`collect()`:

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register(): returns a DuckDB-backed table
library(dplyr) # filter, select, compute, collect

# compute(): run the query and keep the result as a table inside DuckDB
lmdb_cohort <- read_register("lmdb") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010) %>% # reduce rows first - compute() is not a shortcut
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>% # reduce columns first
  compute()

# lmdb_cohort is still lazy: you can keep filtering and joining on it,
# and every later query reads the stored result instead of the whole register.
# collect() only at the end, once the result is small:
statins <- lmdb_cohort %>%
  filter(substr(atc, 1, 4) == "C10A") %>%
  collect()
```

| | `collect()` | `compute()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where the result ends up | an R data frame in R's memory | a temporary table inside DuckDB |
| What you can do next | anything in R | more dplyr verbs, then `collect()` |
| Use it when | the result is small and you are ready to analyse | the result is large, or several later queries start from it |

`compute()` does not make the data disappear: DuckDB still holds the result in
the server's memory until your R session ends. It only saves you from copying it
into R as well, and from re-reading the whole register for every later query. So
the rule above still applies: `filter()` and `select()` first.

It works on the DuckDB-backed tables that `read_register()` and
`read_parquet_duckdb()` give you. On an `open_dataset()` table (arrow), add
`to_duckdb()` before `compute()`.

::: {.callout-note}
**Later: keeping only your cohort.** Once you have built a study population, you
will usually want only your cohort's people from a register. That is done with
[`semi_join()`](function-guide.qmd#semi-join) against your cohort's `pnr`, and
it first matters once the cohort exists ([Phase
10](build-study-population.qmd)).
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Never write an actual CPR number (pnr) in your code.** Use only variable names
and vectors. A CPR number identifies a person, and a script is the file you are
most likely to show a colleague or bring home.
:::

<details>
<summary>What `!!` means, and when you need it</summary>

Sometimes you filter on a **list you defined in R yourself** - typically a set of ICD or year codes:

```r
my_codes <- c("DE10", "DE11", "DE14")   # local R vector you created
register %>% filter(substr(c_diag, 1, 4) %in% !!my_codes)   # first 4 characters, so DE109, DE112 ... also match
```

The lazy query is not executed by R, but by the database engine (Arrow/DuckDB), which runs *separately* from R and does not know your local variables. When the query is built, dplyr checks each name: if the register has a *column* called `my_codes`, it uses the column; if not, it looks up the R vector `my_codes` and copies its values into the query. So the code above usually works without `!!` too. The risk is a name clash: if your local variable has the same name as a column (e.g. a local `year` and the register's `year` column), the column silently wins. `!!` removes that ambiguity - it means: *"this is an R object, not a column name - look up its values in R and use them in the query."*

::: {.callout-tip}
Rule of thumb: if you refer to a **column** in the register, write the name directly. If you refer to an **R variable** you created yourself, putting `!!` in front of it is a recommended safeguard against a name clash.
:::

The other place this comes up is subsetting a register to your cohort's `pnr`. There you use `semi_join()`, which takes an ordinary local table and avoids `!!` entirely. See [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd).

</details>

## Check: do you have data or just a connection?

Many errors come from believing you have fetched data when you still have an
unsent query. Ask the object what it is:

```r
class(my_object)
```

  | What `class()` returns    | What it means       | What to do              |
  | ------------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------- |
  | `"tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"` (and no `"prudent_duckplyr_df"`) | Data is in R        | Nothing - you are ready |
  | `"prudent_duckplyr_df" "duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"` | Unsent DuckDB query (from `read_parquet_duckdb()`, and from `read_register()` in fastreg 0.14.3 or newer) | Add `%>% collect()`     |
  | `"tbl_duckdb_connection"` ... | Unsent DuckDB query (from `to_duckdb()`, and from `read_register()` in fastreg 0.14.2 or older) | Add `%>% collect()`     |
  | `"FileSystemDataset"` ... `"ArrowObject"` | Arrow connection (from `open_dataset()`) | Filter/select, then `%>% collect()` |
  | `"arrow_dplyr_query"`     | Unsent Arrow query  | Add `%>% collect()`     |

Which of the two DuckDB rows you get from `read_register()` depends on the
fastreg version: up to 0.14.2 it opens the parquet with arrow and passes it to
DuckDB, from 0.14.3 it uses duckplyr. Check yours with
`packageVersion("fastreg")`. The duckplyr result says `"data.frame"` even though
nothing has been fetched yet: look for `"prudent_duckplyr_df"`. As long as that
is in the list, the data has not been collected. (`"Table"` is an Arrow table
that is already in memory, which you rarely meet in this guide.)

<details>
<summary>RAM is shared: clean up with `rm()` and `gc()` after large extractions</summary>

On DST all users share the server's memory. When the memory bar in RStudio turns red, it slows everyone's sessions.

```r
rm(large_register)   # removes the object from your R session (disappears from the list in the top right of RStudio)
gc()                 # frees memory R no longer uses, so it can be handed back
```

`rm()` removes the object from your active session - it can no longer be used in code and disappears from the Environment panel (top right in RStudio).

`gc()` (*garbage collection*) does not affect your session - all your other objects are still there. R normally holds on to freed memory a little longer, because it is faster to reuse than to request new memory from the operating system. `gc()` makes R free that memory now, so it can be returned to the operating system and become available to other users on the shared DST server (how much is actually handed back, and when, depends on the system). You lose nothing - it helps your colleagues.

</details>

## The pattern as a diagram {#what-happens-visually}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    P[("Parquet register<br>on the DST server")]:::store
    L["open_dataset()"]:::lazy
    F["filter() - choose rows"]:::lazy
    S["select() - choose columns"]:::lazy
    J["inner_join() - link (optional)"]:::lazy
    C(["collect()"]):::collect
    R[("data.frame in R")]:::store
    V["saveRDS() → datasets/"]:::save

    P -->|"lazy - nothing moves yet"| L
    L --> F --> S --> J
    J -->|"send the query"| C
    C -->|"only chosen rows + columns"| R
    R --> V

    classDef store fill:#eef0f2,stroke:#8a94a6,color:#1f2733;
    classDef lazy fill:#eaf2fb,stroke:#4a78b5,color:#173a5e;
    classDef collect fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e69500,color:#7a4f00;
    classDef save fill:#e9f7ef,stroke:#3fae6b,color:#14532d;
```

The blue steps are lazy: they only build up a query. Data moves into R only at
`collect()` (orange), which is why `filter()` and `select()` must come before
it.

[]{#arrow-vs-duckdb}

<details>
<summary>Parquet, Arrow and DuckDB: what each one is and when each is used</summary>

You do not need to know these names to use the pattern above, but here is what happens under the hood.

**Parquet** is a file format that stores data *column by column* rather than row by row. If you only want `pnr` and `year`, the computer reads only those two columns - not the rest. That is why it is fast. Getting your registers into parquet is covered on [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet).

**Arrow** and **DuckDB** are the two engines that run your query against the parquet. Both are lazy and both end at `collect()`, so your code looks the same either way. The difference is coverage:

| | Arrow | DuckDB |
|---|---|---|
| You get one from | `open_dataset()` | `read_register()` (fastreg), or `to_duckdb()` |
| Speed | fast at reading parquet | also very fast |
| dplyr coverage | does not support every function | supports almost all of them |

To move an Arrow connection over to DuckDB, pipe through `to_duckdb()` (from the `arrow` package):

```r
bef <- open_dataset("path/to/bef/") %>% to_duckdb()   # now queried by DuckDB
```

`read_register()` hands you a DuckDB-backed table already, so this step is built in and you do not call `to_duckdb()` yourself.

If you hit an error about an *"unsupported function"* in Arrow, that is the coverage gap: switch to DuckDB with `to_duckdb()`, or `collect()` into R first and do the operation there.

</details>
